'''Lucio Frydman''' ({{Langx|he|לוסיו פרידמן}}; born 1965) is an Argentine-Israeli chemist whose research focuses on [[magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI), [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) and [[Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance|solid-state NMR]]. He was awarded the 2000 [[Günther Laukien Prize]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.enc-conference.org/LaukienRecipients/PastRecipients/tabid/73/Default.aspx |title=Past Laukien Prize Recipients |publisher=Experimental Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Conference |access-date=3 December 2017}}</ref> the 2013 [[Russell Varian Prize]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20130801005212/en/Agilent-Technologies-Awards-Russell-Varian-Prize-Innovation |title= Agilent Technologies Awards Russell Varian Prize for Innovation in NMR to Dr. Lucio Frydman |date=1 August 2013 |publisher=BusinessWire |access-date=3 December 2017}}</ref> the 2021 [[Ernst Prize]],<ref name="Weizmann Wonder">{{cite web | url=https://wis-wander.weizmann.ac.il/people-and-events/prof-lucio-frydman | title=Weizmann Wonder | date=5 July 2021 | access-date=5 July 2021}}</ref> and the 2025 [[Herbert P. Broida Award]] of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/award/herbert-broida-award |title=Herbert P. Broida Award - APS |access-date=2 April 2025}}</ref> He is Professor in the Department of Chemical and Biological Physics at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] in Israel<ref name="Weizmann Institute">{{cite web |url=http://www.weizmann.ac.il/chemphys/ |title=Department of Chemical & Biological Physics |publisher=Weizmann Institute |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref> and Chief Scientist in Chemistry and Biology at the US [[National High Magnetic Field Laboratory]] in [[Tallahassee]], Florida.<ref name=MagLab2012>{{cite web |url=https://nationalmaglab.org/news-events/news/lucio-frydman-tapped-as-magnet-lab-chemistry-biology-chief-scientist |title=Lucio Frydman Tapped as Magnet Lab Chemistry/Biology Chief Scientist |publisher=National High Magnetic Field Laboratory |date=27 June 2012 |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref> He is a fellow of the International Society of Magnetic Resonance<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.weizmann.ac.il/ISMAR/ismar-organization#ismar-fellows |title=ISMAR Fellows |publisher=International Society of Magnetic Resonance |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref> and of the International Society of Magnetic Resonance in Medicine.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ismrm.org/22m/fellows/ |title=2022 Fellows of the Society - ISMRM |access-date=29 May 2022}}</ref> He was the Editor-in-Chief of the [[Journal of Magnetic Resonance]] (2011-2021).<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.journals.elsevier.com/journal-of-magnetic-resonance |title=Journal of Magnetic Resonance |publisher=Elsevier |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref>

==Birth and Education==
Frydman was born and raised in [[Buenos Aires]], Argentina, where he completed his undergraduate studies in chemistry in 1986 at the [[University of Buenos Aires]]. In 1990 he received his Ph.D. in chemistry from the same university.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frydman |first1=L |date=2016 |title=In Memorian: Prof. Luis Diaz and the Early Days of Solid State NMR in Argentina |url=http://www.eurekaselect.com/140118 |journal=Current Pharmaceutical Biotechnology |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=480–483 |doi=10.2174/138920101705160303165830 |pmid=27398421 |access-date=5 December 2017 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Career==
In 1990 Frydman started working in his post-doctoral research at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] and at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], under the direction of [[Alexander Pines]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://pines.berkeley.edu/people/alumni |title=PinesLab. Global Pinenuts (Alumni) |publisher=Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref> In 1992 he was appointed Assistant Professor in the Department of Chemistry at the [[University of Illinois at Chicago]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.trustees.uillinois.edu/trustees/resources/historical-files/GrayBook1992.pdf#page=180 |title=University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Academic Personnel 1992-1993 |publisher=University of Illinois |format=PDF |access-date=10 December 2017}}</ref>  where he became Associate Professor in 1996,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.trustees.uillinois.edu/trustees/resources/historical-files/GrayBook1996.pdf#page=48 |title=University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Academic Personnel 1996-1997 |publisher=University of Illinois |format=PDF |access-date=10 December 2017}}</ref>  and Full Professor in 1999.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.trustees.uillinois.edu/trustees/resources/historical-files/GrayBook1999.pdf#page=53 |title=University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Academic Personnel 1999-2000 |publisher=University of Illinois |format=PDF |access-date=10 December 2017}}</ref>  In 2001 Frydman moved to Israel, where he was appointed Professor in the Department of Chemical Physics at the Weizmann Institute of Science. Since 2015 he holds the Bertha and Isadore Gudelsky Professorial Chair; in 2017 Frydman was appointed Head of the newly formed Department of Chemical and Biological Physics.<ref name="Weizmann Institute"/> He was Director of the Fritz Haber Center for Physical Chemistry from 2007 to 2012, and again since 2017.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.weizmann.ac.il/chemphys/fritz-haber-center |title=Fritz Haber Center |publisher=Weizmann Institute |access-date=5 December 2017|date=2016-03-17 }}</ref> He is Director of the Helen and Martin Kimmel Institute for Magnetic Resonance Research since 2012<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/pages/helen-and-martin-kimmel-institute-magnetic-resonance-research |title=The Helen and Martin Kimmel Institute for Magnetic Resonance Research |publisher=Weizmann Institute |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref> and he became the Director of the Clore Institute for High-Field Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Spectroscopy since 2015.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/pages/clore-institute-high-field-magnetic-resonance-imaging-and-spectroscopy |title=The Clore Institute for High-Field Magnetic Resonance Imaging |publisher=Weizmann Institute |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref>
In 2012 Frydman was appointed Chief Scientist in Chemistry and Biology at the US National High Magnetic Field Laboratory in Tallahassee, Florida.<ref name=MagLab2012 />

==Research==
Frydman’s research focuses on the fields of MRI, NMR and solid-state NMR. His scientific work has produced over 200 scientific publications in [[Scholarly peer review|peer-reviewed]] journals.<ref name=GoogleScholar>{{cite web |url=https://scholar.google.co.il/scholar?as_q=&as_epq=&as_oq=&as_eq=&as_occt=any&as_sauthors=Lucio+Frydman&as_publication=&as_ylo=&as_yhi=&hl=en&as_sdt=0%2C5 |title=Articles by Lucio Frydman |publisher=Google Scholar |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref>
In 1995 Frydman and his coworker John Harwood developed the [[Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance#Quadrupolar interaction|Multiple-Quantum Magic-Angle-Spinning]] (MQMAS) NMR experiment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frydman |first1=L |last2=Harwood |first2=JS |date=1995 |title=Isotropic Spectra of Half-Integer Quadrupolar Spins from Bidimensional Magic-Angle Spinning NMR |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=117 |issue=19 |pages=5367–5368 |doi=10.1021/ja00124a023 |bibcode=1995JAChS.117.5367F }}</ref> The article describing this experiment received more than 1000 citations<ref name=GoogleScholar /> and the experiment became widely used for acquiring solid-state NMR spectra of [[Quadrupole|quadrupolar]] nuclei.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Amoureux |first1=JP |last2=Pruski |first2=M |title=Encyclopedia of Magnetic Resonance |chapter=MQMAS NMR: Experimental Strategies and Applications |date=2008  |doi=10.1002/9780470034590.emrstm0319.pub2 |isbn=978-0470034590 }}</ref> 
In 2002 Frydman and his coworkers introduced a new approach to collect NMR data that allows the acquisition of arbitrary multi-dimensional NMR spectra within a single scan.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frydman |first1=L |last2=Scherf |first2=T |last3=Lupulescu |first3=A |date=2002 |title=The Acquisition of Multidimensional NMR Spectra within a Single Scan |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA |volume=99 |issue=25 |pages=15858–15862 |doi=10.1073/pnas.212643599 |pmid=12444260 |pmc=138529 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Provided that sufficient sensitivity is available, this method can yield [[Two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|2D NMR]] correlations that are orders of magnitude faster than hitherto possible and it has found applications in many areas of chemistry.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gouilleux |first1=B |last2=Rouger |first2=L |last3=Giraudeau |first3=P |title=eMagRes |chapter=Ultrafast Multi-dimensional NMR: Principles and Recent Applications |date=2016 |volume=5 |pages=913–922 |doi=10.1002/9780470034590.emrstm1494 |isbn=9780470034590 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/ultrafast-nmr-shows-the-way-/3004131.article |title=Ultrafast NMR Shows the Way |last=Robinson |first=P |date=2 February 2012 |website=Chemistry World |publisher=The Royal Chemical Society |access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref>
Recently, Frydman and his coworkers further developed this spatio-temporal encoding (SPEN) strategy to collect MRI images in a single scan.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Z |last2=Seginer |first2=A |last3=Frydman |first3=L |date=2017 |title=A New Approach to Magnetic Resonance Imaging with Exceptional Resilience to Field Inhomogeneities |journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=623–634 |doi=10.1002/mrm.26145 |pmid=26901840 |pmc=5184846 }}</ref> This method allows the acquisition of real-time MRI spectra and can be used to monitor processes in [[Functional magnetic resonance imaging|functional MRI]] (fMRI) and in [[diffusion MRI]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Solomon |first1=E |last2=Avni |first2=R |last3=Hadas |first3=R |last4=Raz |first4=T |last5=Garbow |first5=JR |last6=Bendel |first6=P |last7=Frydman |first7=L |last8=Neeman |first8=M |date=2014 |title=Major Mouse Placental Compartments Revealed by Diffusion Weighted MRI, Contrast-Enhanced MRI, and Fluorescence Imaging |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA |volume=111 |issue=28 |pages=10353–10358 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1401695111 |pmid=24969421 |pmc=4104865 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11110353S |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.israel21c.org/using-mri-to-detect-fetal-distress/ |title=Using MRI to detect fetal distress |last=Press |first=VS |date=15 October 2014 |website=Israel21C News Magazine |publisher=Israel21C |access-date=6 December 2017}}</ref>
